## Method

Leave-last-out. For every player with **>= 3 bookings**, hide the most recent
booking, rank the catalogue from what remains, and ask whether the hidden venue came back
in the top 5. Four arms rank the *same* candidate set:

| arm | what it is |
|---|---|
| random | a seeded permutation — the floor any ranking must clear |
| popularity | the wave's named baseline: `0.7 x log booked-count + 0.3 x rating`, no personal signal |
| cold-start (as served) | popularity blended with the player's stated sports — **what the app actually falls back to**, and the baseline the lift claim is made against |
| content model | cosine of the venue matrix against the recency-weighted user profile — the shipped path |

Two cohorts are reported. **All items** keeps every eligible player. **Novel venues only**
drops the players whose hidden venue already appears in their trimmed history: a repeat
visit sits next to its own profile vector and is close to free, so the honest headline is
the cohort where the model has to generalise to a venue the player has never booked.

The high-review list is filtered against the hidden venue before scoring — leaving it in
would leak the answer through the affinity block.

## Are the percentages honest? (match-% spread)

Every percentage the top-5 rails would have printed across the evaluated population:

| min | p10 | median | p90 | max | distinct values | percentages sampled |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 79% | 82% | 89% | 95% | 98% | 20 | 1020 |

`match% = 55 + 43 x cosine`, so the reachable range is
55-98%. A rail of 97-99% would mean the number carries no
information; the spread above is the evidence that it does.

Read the floor correctly: this samples the **top 5 rows only**, i.e. the highest
percentages the app ever prints. It is not the distribution over the whole catalogue, which
runs lower — the claim being evidenced here is that the rail's own numbers vary, not that
low percentages exist somewhere.

## Why 0.5 history / 0.3 stated / 0.2 affinity?

Same test, same population, only the user-vector blend varies. (The sweep rebinds the
weight dict in memory; the frozen feature file is never edited, so the fingerprint stays
`138790ba577ea0f0`.)

| history | stated | affinity | HitRate@5 | MRR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.98 | 0.01 | 0.01 | 0.472 | 0.223 |
| 0.70 | 0.20 | 0.10 | 0.494 | 0.238 |
| 0.60 | 0.30 | 0.10 | 0.483 | 0.255 |
| 0.50 | 0.30 | 0.20 | 0.461  ← **shipped** | 0.250 |
| 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.20 | 0.461 | 0.263 |
| 0.34 | 0.33 | 0.33 | 0.449 | 0.260 |
| 0.20 | 0.60 | 0.20 | 0.506 | 0.277 |

The grid spans 0.056 on HitRate@5 over n = 89 held-out players, where one player is 1.1 points and the binomial standard error at p = 0.461 is +/-0.053 (5.3 points). **Every row therefore sits inside one standard error of every other one.** The finding is that the model is insensitive to this blend at this sample size — not that the shipped split is optimal.

The nominal best row (0.20/0.60/0.20, 0.506) is 0.045 ahead — inside the noise, so it is not a reason to change anything.

So why keep history at the front? Because history is the only block that separates two players who ticked the same sport, and a rail that is identical for everyone who plays cricket is not a recommendation. The sweep is what should decide this, and it cannot yet; re-run it once the real corpus has enough evaluable players to separate the rows, and ship the winner if the ordering survives.

## Cold-start guard

18 of the evaluated players have no bookings, no high reviews and no stated sport — a zero profile vector, where cosine similarity is undefined rather than small. Every probed one took the popularity branch and returned a full rail (profile: `cold_start`), so the guard holds on this population and no personalised percentage is claimed for them.

## What this evaluation cannot tell you

- **The synthetic players are simulated.** Venue attributes, per-venue demand and booking
  dates all come from the frozen S.3 world, but the *user* layer is generated here (taste
  weights are printed in `reco_eval_metrics.json` under `config.taste`). It measures the
  ranking function on a population whose ground-truth preference is known — not real
  Pakistani players' behaviour.
- **The simulated world has no amenities and no street addresses**, so the amenity block
  is inert there and `zone` collapses to a city token. Those two blocks are only exercised
  by the real corpus, which is too small to measure them.
- **Precision@5 is HitRate@5 / 5** by construction under a single-item holdout. It is
  reported because the wave asks for it; MRR is the metric that adds information.
- **The catalogue is small.** 20 synthetic venues means a random top-5 list hits
  25% of the time *by construction* (5/20), which is why the lift that matters is
  the one over cold-start, not the one over random. As the real catalogue grows that floor
  drops and every arm's absolute numbers will fall with it — compare arms within a run,
  never HitRate@5 across runs on different catalogues.
- **No online evidence.** Nobody has clicked anything. Whether a higher HitRate@5 converts
  into more bookings is an A/B question the platform has no traffic for yet.
